title: The Nazareth manifesto (Luke 4:14–21)
hookLine: he unrolls Isaiah: good news to the poor, sight to the blind, freedom for the oppressed
tomorrow: to the edge of the cliff

cards: A small-town synagogue on the sabbath. Everyone knows everyone. Today the young man who was brought up here, Joseph's son, is back, and word about him has spread through the region.
Luke says he went into the synagogue on the sabbath day, "as his custom was." He stands up to read. The attendant hands him a scroll, the prophet Isaiah.

And Luke slows down for a detail: he unrolls it, looking for a particular place. He's choosing his words. Luke has said he was already teaching in synagogues, but this is the first time Luke lets us hear what he says.

teach.h: THE SPIRIT OF THE LORD IS UPON ME.
teach.b: He reads, in the King James words: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised, To preach the acceptable year of the Lord."
Count who's in it. The poor. The brokenhearted.
The captives. The blind. The bruised, the crushed and oppressed.

teach.h: FIVE KINDS OF PEOPLE, NONE POWERFUL.
teach.b: Five kinds of people, and not one of them powerful. That's why some readers call this the Nazareth manifesto: a mission statement, read out at the start.
Some hear in the acceptable year of the Lord an echo of the jubilee in Leviticus, the fiftieth year, when liberty was proclaimed and land went back to its families.

teach.h: HE SAT DOWN; EVERY EYE ON HIM.
teach.b: Then: "And he closed the book, and he gave it again to the minister, and sat down. And the eyes of all them that were in the synagogue were fastened on him." Everyone waits.
Then one sentence: "This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears."

teach.h: THIS DAY IS THIS SCRIPTURE FULFILLED IN YOUR EARS.
teach.b: Not someday, for those five kinds of people: now, in the room where they're sitting.

And a quiet detail you can check: set Luke beside Isaiah 61, and he stops reading mid-verse, just before Isaiah's next words, the day of vengeance of our God. Christians read that pause in different ways, but it's there.

how: Some Christian groups working with the poor, prisoners and the sick point to Luke 4:18–19 as their charter, and in the Revised Common Lectionary the passage is read in the season after Epiphany.

games.q: you're reading Isaiah 61 aloud in your hometown synagogue. the next words are about a day of vengeance. what do you do?
o: read on to the end of the chapter.
stop, close the book, sit down, and say it's fulfilled today.
games.why: he stops just before the day of vengeance, closes the book, sits down, and says: this day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears.

practice: Let the five come back slowly, waiting a breath with each: the poor; the brokenhearted, grieving or lonely; the captive, stuck in debt, in prison, in a habit; the blind, who can't see a way forward; the bruised, pushed down by others.
Notice if one of them has a face, someone you actually know or pass every week, and hold them there with care. If you pray, hold that person before God; if not, simply hold them in mind.

wordCard.voice: Jubilee. The Levitical year of liberty and land returned, echoed in the acceptable year of the Lord that Jesus read about himself.

orig.note: Greek: release, letting go. in Luke 4:18 it stands behind both deliverance and liberty.

carryVoice: Your line: today this is fulfilled. Good news for the five, not someday. See you tomorrow.

And he closed the book, and he gave it again to the minister, and sat down. And the eyes of all them that were in the synagogue were fastened on him.
This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears.
